archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first, opportunistic defense)
archetype.definition: A Burrow-led offense that throws more than anyone relative to the situation, paired with a defense that has jumped from the league's basement to the top half on the strength of its pass rush and pass coverage, good enough to win the division but not yet a complete team.

report.headline: The defense finally showed up; the run defense and third downs still haven't.
report.take:
Cincinnati at 3-2 is about what its play deserves. Win expectation is essentially zero (-0.01), the point differential is +3.8 a game, and net EPA ranks sixth. Nothing here is a fluke record. What has changed is the shape of the team. The last two seasons ended with the defense 27th and 29th in EPA allowed, and the 2025 unit gave up 28.9 points a game. This year it sits 11th overall and sixth against the pass, with 17 sacks (third) and a sack rate fourth in the league. That turnaround is the whole story of why a 6-11 team looks like a contender again.

The offense is built around Burrow's arm and his clock. Cincinnati's pass rate over expected is the highest in the league at +6.9, and the pocket is a problem: the line ranks 23rd in pressure allowed. Burrow handles it with the 30th-ranked time to throw, a 2.57-second release that keeps the sack rate seventh-best. The passing attack has also been climbing. After negative pass EPA in each of the first two weeks it posted +14.7, +7.4 and +13.9 over the last three. Higgins (43 targets) has edged Chase (38) as the top target, and Chase Brown's 28 targets make him a real third option. The run game is functional rather than good. A 3.65 yards-per-carry average is mediocre, but the line ranks third in stuff rate and second on short-yardage conversions, so it gets the hard yards when it has to.

The defense's numbers hide two things. First, the takeaways are lumpy: seven of the nine came in two games, four against Tampa and three against a Miami offense that ranks 30th. Second, the unit bends a lot. It allows conversions on 46% of third downs (28th), misses tackles at the 26th-worst rate, ranks 30th in explosive runs allowed, and is 28th against short passes. What has kept points down is a 41% red-zone touchdown rate, third-best in the league, and that kind of rate tends to drift toward average. Miami ran for 217 yards in Week 5, and Houston threw for 353 in Week 2 and still scored only 6. That is a defense living on sacks and red-zone stops.

The direction is still positive. The schedule ahead includes Tennessee, New Orleans, Washington, Indianapolis and Cleveland twice, and the pass offense is trending up. A 10-win season is the reasonable center. The division likely runs through Baltimore, though, and the Ravens' run game hits exactly the part of this defense that hasn't been fixed.

strengths.title: A real pass rush, finally
strengths.body: Cincinnati gets home on 8.7% of dropbacks, fourth in the league, and pairs that with the sixth-best pass EPA allowed. That is the backbone of the jump from 29th in defensive EPA last year. Sack rates are steadier than turnover luck, so this part should hold.

strengths.title: Burrow's quick game beats protection
strengths.body: The line allows pressure at a 23rd-ranked rate, but Burrow's 2.57-second release keeps the sack rate seventh-best. The staff leans into it with the league's highest pass rate over expected. The air attack has produced double-digit pass EPA in two of the last three games, including 428 yards against Jacksonville's third-ranked defense.

strengths.title: Wins the hard yards up front
strengths.body: The run game averages only 3.65 a carry, but the line rarely gets blown up in the backfield. It ranks third in stuff rate and converts 90% of short-yardage tries. That keeps drives alive even when the ground game isn't creating chunk plays.

concerns.title: Run defense leaks big plays
concerns.body: Cincinnati ranks 24th in rush EPA allowed and 30th in explosive runs allowed, and tackles poorly (26th in missed-tackle rate). Miami's 30th-ranked offense ran for 217 yards. This is a structural flaw rather than noise, and run-heavy opponents will keep testing it.

concerns.title: Bend-don't-break may break
concerns.body: The defense allows 46% on third down (28th) and gets torched on short passes (28th). It has survived on a red-zone TD rate that ranks third. Red-zone defense regresses, so expect points allowed to creep up unless the third-down numbers improve.

concerns.title: Turnover margin is front-loaded
concerns.body: Nine takeaways rank third, but seven came in two games, including three against a bottom-three Miami offense. The +0.8 turnover margin per game props up the scoring margin and is unlikely to hold at this pace.

trend.note: Pass EPA went from -2.6 and -0.5 in the first two weeks to +14.7, +7.4 and +13.9 over the last three. The offense has found its rhythm even though the record split 1-2 over that stretch. The defense's results have swung with its takeaway count.

nextGame.headline: Rested Bengals at Baltimore: Burrow's deep shots vs the Ravens' ground game
nextGame.body:
Baltimore is the better team on paper, fifth in net EPA with the sixth-ranked offense. It plays to the Bengals' weak spot. The Ravens sit 27th in pass rate over expected, run for 4.8 a carry (fourth), and rank sixth in rush EPA, while Cincinnati is 24th against the run and 30th in explosive runs allowed. The flip side is the Ravens' 19th-ranked defense. It is excellent underneath (third in short-pass EPA) but 25th on deep throws, and it gets little pressure (28th). That should give Burrow time to push the ball to Higgins, and Baltimore has been the league's second-worst defense against opposing WR1s by EPA per target. Cincinnati also comes off a bye, with 14 days of rest.

Availability is the swing. Lamar Jackson missed Week 5 with an ankle sprain, Tyler Huntley started, and Jackson's estimated return date falls before this game. Center Cam Jurgens (concussion) and edge Trey Hendrickson (finger) carry similar estimates, and Hendrickson matters because Baltimore's rush is already thin. Tight end Durham Smythe is on IR, which blunts a matchup Cincinnati usually loses, since it ranks 29th against TE1s. The Bengals' own report is all depth players: Hudson, Dugger and Young each played 26% of snaps or less. Weather isn't in the forecast yet, and the line isn't posted.

keyMatchups.title: Ravens run game vs leaky front
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore's efficient, run-first offense meets a Cincinnati defense that gives up explosive runs and misses tackles. If the Ravens stay on schedule, Cincinnati's third-down defense, already 28th, will be under constant stress. This is the matchup most likely to decide the game.

keyMatchups.title: Burrow deep vs soft Raven safeties
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore shuts down the short game but bleeds on deep balls and allows 0.76 EPA per target to opposing WR1s. Burrow's habit of getting the ball out quickly plays into the Ravens' strength. He'll need to hold it a beat longer and attack downfield, which the weak Baltimore pass rush should allow.

keyMatchups.title: Lamar's ankle
keyMatchups.body: Jackson's status changes this game. With him, Baltimore's fifth-ranked pass offense and run game are both at full strength. With Huntley, Cincinnati's pass rush, which ranks fourth in sack rate, gets a far better shot at forcing mistakes.

nextGame.watch: Baltimore's early-down rushing success. If the Ravens are gaining four-plus yards on first down, Cincinnati's defense loses its pass-rush leverage and the game tilts Baltimore's way.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying profile supports a winning season. The record matches the point differential, the passing game is trending up, and the remaining schedule is soft outside of Kansas City and two Baltimore games. Tennessee, New Orleans, Washington and Indianapolis all rank 22nd or worse on at least one side of the ball. The sack-driven pass defense should hold up, and Burrow's quick-game approach has kept a shaky line from becoming a liability.

What will regress is the defense's luck at the margins. The red-zone touchdown rate and the takeaway pace are both elite and both fragile, and the third-down and run-defense numbers suggest points allowed will drift up toward 23-24 a game. Expect the offense to carry more of the load in the second half, with the division likely settled in the Week 17 rematch against Baltimore.
swingFactors: Whether run defense and tackling improve against run-heavy opponents
Red-zone defense regressing toward league average
Lamar Jackson's health in the two Baltimore games

confidence.note: Five games; the defensive turnaround leans partly on red-zone stops and clustered takeaways, and the next opponent's QB is uncertain.
